title: Helping Children Open Up About Their Feelings
intro: Warmth, curiosity, and listening help children feel safe to share. Discover simple ways to welcome every feeling and create meaningful everyday conversations.
sections: Simple Ways to Create Meaningful Conversations Every Day

One of the greatest gifts we can give our children is the feeling that they can come to us with anything. When children know they will be met with warmth, curiosity, and understanding, not judgment, they become more willing to share their thoughts, feelings, and experiences. These everyday conversations strengthen trust, build emotional awareness, and help children feel less alone. Here are a few simple ways to create a home where feelings are welcome.
Start by Observing

Before asking questions, take a moment to simply watch your child. Notice their facial expressions, body language, energy level, and what they're doing. Sometimes children tell us how they're feeling long before they find the words. You may also notice that your child naturally opens up at certain times of the day, during bedtime, while drawing, in the car, or during play. Instead of expecting conversations to happen on demand, try meeting your child in the moments when they're most ready to share.
Every Feeling Is Welcome

There are no bad feelings. Joy, excitement, sadness, fear, frustration, jealousy, disappointment, and anger all have something important to tell us. Rather than trying to make difficult feelings disappear, we can help children understand them and find healthy ways to express them. Even anger has an important purpose. It often tells us that something we care about feels unfair, threatened, or lost. The goal isn't to get rid of anger, it's to help children express it safely and respectfully.
Listen Before You Solve

When children share something difficult, our first instinct is often to fix the problem. But most of the time, what children need first is to feel heard. Listening without rushing to offer advice helps children feel understood and teaches them that their feelings matter. Once they feel emotionally safe, they're often much more open to guidance and problem-solving.
Feelings Live in the Body

Children often notice physical sensations before they recognize an emotion. A tight tummy, heavy shoulders, a racing heart, or warm cheeks can all be clues that something is happening inside. Helping children notice these body signals builds emotional awareness and makes it easier for them to understand what they're experiencing.
Tears Are Part of Healing

When children cry, they're not doing something wrong. Tears are one of the body's natural ways of processing disappointment, sadness, frustration, and change. Instead of trying to stop the tears, we can stay close, offer comfort, and remind children that they don't have to go through difficult feelings alone.
Create a Safe Place to Share

Children are far more likely to keep talking when they know they won't be met with criticism, shame, or punishment. If a child shares something difficult, try listening first. Advice, limits, or problem-solving can always come later. Protecting these moments of connection teaches children that home is a safe place to bring their whole emotional world.
Ask Curious Questions
Sometimes children don't know exactly what they're feeling. Curious questions invite children to explore their emotions without feeling corrected or misunderstood.
Children Learn by Watching Us

One of the most powerful ways to teach emotional expression is by modeling it ourselves. Share your own feelings in simple, age-appropriate ways: “I felt disappointed today.” “I was nervous before my meeting, but taking a few deep breaths helped me.” When children see adults talking openly and calmly about emotions, they learn that feelings are a normal part of everyday life.
Remember: Every Feeling Has Something to Tell Us

Behind every emotion is something that matters. Instead of asking, “How can I make this feeling go away?”, try asking: “What might this feeling be trying to tell me?” When children learn to listen to their feelings instead of fearing them, they develop emotional awareness, confidence, and resilience that will support them throughout life.

title: Discover Heartly’s Pocket of Feelings
intro: Explore how Heartly’s Pocket of Feelings brings play and connection into everyday moments, helping children share what they feel and discover ways to cope with their emotions.
sections: Helping Children Talk About Feelings Through Story, Play, and Connection

Children experience a wide range of emotions, from excitement and joy to worry, frustration, sadness, and everything in between. All of these feelings are a natural part of growing up. But finding the words to describe them isn’t always easy. That’s why we created Heartly’s Pocket of Feelings. This playful gift set helps children recognize, express, and share their feelings through stories, imaginative play, and meaningful conversations with the grownups they love. At FeelieBees, we believe emotional growth begins with connection. When children feel safe sharing their inner world, they have opportunities to understand themselves, feel heard, and build trusting relationships with the people who care for them.
Why Talking About Feelings Matters

One of the greatest gifts we can offer children is the reassurance that they can come to us with any feeling. When children share something about a difficult day, an exciting adventure, or a moment that hurt their feelings, they begin making sense of their experiences. A caring adult who listens with warmth and curiosity can help them feel understood and less alone. These conversations don’t need to be long or carefully planned. They can happen during play, while reading together, or in a quiet moment at the end of the day. What matters is making room for what the child wants to share, without pressuring them to explain everything or trying to fix how they feel.
A Story, a Cuddly Friend, and Ways to Cope with Feelings

Heartly’s Pocket of Feelings includes a storybook, a Heartly fox plush, 9 interchangeable feeling hearts, and 9 emotion cards. Together, they help children explore and share their feelings, while discovering ways to cope with them.
📖 Begin with Heartly’s Story

Heartly’s story introduces children to nine feelings through relatable adventures. Reading together offers a gentle way to notice emotions and talk about them without putting the child in the spotlight. You might pause and ask: “Have you ever felt something like that?” There’s no need to turn every page into a question. Sometimes simply enjoying the story together is enough. Children may return to a scene or share something later, when they feel ready.
🦊 Let Heartly Help Start the Conversation

A familiar plush friend can give children another way to explore what’s happening inside. Children can choose a feeling heart from Heartly’s pocket and place it on his chest. They might choose a feeling from the story, imagine how Heartly feels, or pick one that matches their own experience. Instead of asking a direct question like “How are you feeling?”, you could try: “What happened that made Heartly feel worried today?” or “What do you think would help Heartly right now?” Talking about Heartly may feel easier than talking about themselves. If a child shares something through him, follow their lead with curiosity. There’s no need to interpret their play or assume that every feeling they give Heartly is their own. Heartly can also join in pretend play about new experiences, such as starting school, visiting the doctor, or trying a new activity. Acting out a situation together gives children room to ask questions and explore different feelings at their own pace.
❤️ Explore the Emotion Cards Together

Each emotion card introduces a feeling and offers simple, child-friendly ways to cope with it. The aim isn’t to make a feeling disappear. It’s to remind children that all feelings are natural and welcome, while exploring ways to express them safely and find support when needed. After choosing a feeling heart, you can look at the matching card together. Notice the illustration, talk about the feeling, and see whether any of the coping ideas appeal to the child. You can also come up with your own: “What helps you when you feel this way?” Parents, caregivers, and educators can use these moments to listen and discover what feels supportive for each child.
Make Room for Their Own Way of Playing

There’s no single right way to use Heartly. Some children may want to talk, while others prefer to act out a story, cuddle the plush, or quietly choose a heart. They don’t need to name a feeling correctly or explain why they chose it. Let the set be an invitation. A warm, interested presence matters more than following every step or having a particular conversation.
More Than a Toy

Heartly’s Pocket of Feelings is an invitation to slow down, play together, and make room for children’s emotional worlds. Whether at home or in an educational setting, these small moments offer a simple message: your feelings matter, and you don’t have to face them alone.

title: Helping Children Through Frustration
intro: Learning to notice, name, and talk about feelings is a skill children can practise in small, playful ways.
sections: Start with noticing
A quick heartbeat, a big smile, or tight little fists can be clues to a feeling. Help your child notice these clues with curiosity and without judgment.
Build a feelings vocabulary
Begin with familiar words like happy, sad, and angry. As your child grows, explore words like disappointed, proud, and worried through stories and conversation.
Practise perspective-taking
Pause during a story and wonder together: ‘How might this character feel? What could a kind friend do?’ There doesn’t have to be only one answer.
Keep it playful
Use pictures, pretend play, and drawing to explore feelings. Follow your child’s interest and let them choose whether they want to talk.

title: Why Punishment Doesn't Build Cooperation
intro: You don’t need a perfect plan to make space for feelings. Try these simple activities with materials you already have at home.
sections: Draw your weather
Ask, ‘If your feelings were the weather today, what would they look like?’ Draw sunshine, clouds, rainbows, or a brand-new kind of weather together.
Play feelings charades
Take turns making a face or striking a pose. Guess the feeling together, then talk about when someone might feel that way.
Make a kindness jar
Write or draw little acts of kindness on scraps of paper. Pick one together: give a hug if someone wants one, share a toy, or say thank you.
Try a Heartly colouring break
Print a free activity, grab some crayons, and slow down together. Invite conversation without turning the activity into a quiz.
